editorNote: COMDEX has grown from a dealer gathering into an industry city, and nearly every aisle now bends toward the IBM PC. Beyond Las Vegas, floppy-disk fiction and fiercely priced home computers are making the holiday shelf every bit as consequential as the trade-show floor.
morningLine: IBM compatibility commands COMDEX while interactive fiction and home computers contest the Christmas shelf.

lead.headline: COMDEX Becomes Las Vegas's Biggest Show as IBM Compatibility Takes Command
lead.dek: More than 80,000 visitors and 1,400 exhibitors gather around a market increasingly organized by the IBM PC standard.
body: The computer trade has taken over Las Vegas. A show that began in the winter of 1979 with roughly 4,000 visitors has swollen to more than 80,000 attendees, filling the convention center and rooms in five major hotels. Its 1,400 exhibitors include 400 newcomers, with AT&T among the names making a first appearance.

Yet the loudest message is not a revolutionary new box. Contemporary reporting finds most of the machines on display to be variations on the IBM Personal Computer design. Future Computing analyst Portia Isaacson puts the trend plainly: “The architecture of the IBM PC has become the industry standard.” Compatibility is becoming the language in which makers court dealers and buyers.

That shift changes the character of the show. Software and marketing are displacing the hobbyist hardware experiments that once supplied much of the excitement. Elaborate multistory booths compete for attention, and a serious display can cost tens of thousands of dollars. Hewlett-Packard expects to recruit hundreds of dealers for its new desktop system.

Windows draw the strongest crowds. VisiCorp demonstrates Visi On joining word processing, financial planning and graphing on a screen divided into separate panes. The industry arrives without a singular hardware sensation, but it leaves a clear direction: the IBM-compatible marketplace, stocked with graphical software and dealer support, is becoming personal computing’s commercial center.

stories.headline: Interactive Fiction Turns the Floppy Disk into a Bestseller Shelf
body: TIME this week treats text adventures as a new kind of software bestseller: stories in which the reader types commands, questions suspects and redirects the plot. Its opening scene comes from Infocom’s Deadline, where evidence and contradictory testimony turn the keyboard into a detective’s notebook.

Infocom’s The Witness carries the idea into a 1930s Los Angeles murder mystery. A December COMPUTE! review finds a world assembled through prose rather than arcade graphics, asking the player to examine rooms, objects and alibis closely.

The genre also solves a stubborn commercial problem. A portable text engine can carry the same tale across otherwise incompatible microcomputer families. On a crowded holiday shelf, the floppy disk is becoming a place for authored worlds as well as utilities and scores.

stories.headline: Home Computers Move to the Center of the Christmas Battle
body: The home computer has become one of the defining gifts of Christmas 1983. Atari, Commodore, Coleco and IBM are fighting for attention with sharply different combinations of price, memory, storage and bundled peripherals.

Antic’s holiday guide puts Atari’s 16K 600XL at $199 and the 64K 800XL at $299, both with BASIC built in. The $449 Atari 1050 drive brings enhanced-density disks and DOS 3.0, while touch tablets promise drawing and a more direct way to work on screen.

Coleco’s Adam counters with a bundled computer, data drive and daisy-wheel printer. IBM’s PCjr, announced in November but due to ship in early 1984, hangs over the season as a future entrant. Buyers are choosing not just a machine, but a family of software, storage and accessories.

stories.headline: Windows Become Software’s New Battleground
body: The busiest COMDEX demonstrations split a single screen into windows, allowing different programs or views to remain visible at once. Visi On places writing, calculations and graphs inside a mouse-driven environment for IBM-compatible machines.
The idea promises relief from the ritual of closing one task before opening another, but the price of admission is steep. Visi On demands an expensive, well-equipped PC by home-computer standards.

Even so, this week’s attention suggests that the next contest will not be decided by processor specifications alone. Software makers are now competing to define how people see, point to and move among their work.
